name: LP5036RJVR
title: LP5030, LP5036: 30- and 36-channel 12-bit PWM I2C RGB LED drivers with ultra-low quiescent current
summary: LP5030 and LP5036 are constant-current sink LED drivers with 30 or 36 outputs, grouped in threes for RGB modules. Each output has its own 8-bit colour register and each RGB module its own 8-bit intensity register, which combine into a 12-bit, 29 kHz PWM per output; three banks let one write fade many modules together. One resistor sets the full-scale current, up to 25.5 mA per output from 2.7 V or 35 mA from 3.3 V. The device runs from 2.7 V to 5.5 V, talks I2C at up to 400 kHz with four selectable addresses plus broadcast, and falls to 12 µA maximum in automatic power-save and 1 µA in shutdown.
key_figures: 25.5 mA max per channel over full VCC; 35 mA max per channel at VCC ≥ 3.3 V

circuits.title: Simplified schematic
circuits.description: One LP5036 lighting twelve RGB modules. Each module's red, green and blue LEDs sit on three consecutive outputs (OUT0 to OUT2 for LED0, on up to OUT33 to OUT35 for LED11), cathode to the OUT pin and anode to the LED rail VLED, so each output sinks one LED's current. A controller drives EN, SDA and SCL; SDA and SCL each have a pull-up to the controller's supply VMCU. ADDR0 and ADDR1 are both grounded, which gives address 011 0000. CVCC decouples VCC, CVCAP holds up the internal regulator at VCAP, and RIREF from IREF to ground sets the full-scale current of every channel.

parts.note: RIREF; 4900 Ω sets 15 mA full scale

notes: RIREF = 105 × 0.7 V / ISET; 4.9 kΩ gives 15 mA.
Pull-ups of 1.8 kΩ to 4.7 kΩ are usual, picked to suit line capacitance, logic voltage and bit rate.

circuits.title: Two LP5036 on one I2C bus
circuits.description: Two LP5036 share the controller's EN, SDA and SCL lines and one pair of pull-ups to VMCU, driving 24 RGB modules between them. They differ only in their address pins: U1 has ADDR0 and ADDR1 grounded (address 011 0000), U2 has ADDR0 on VVCC and ADDR1 grounded (address 011 0001). Each device has its own CVCC, CVCAP and RIREF, and its 36 outputs sink the cathodes of twelve RGB modules whose anodes are on VLED. Up to four devices can share a bus this way.

operation.text: A constant-current sink driver with 30 (LP5030) or 36 (LP5036) outputs, built for RGB LEDs. It contains its own regulator, a 15 MHz oscillator and an I2C slave; one resistor on IREF sets the full-scale current for all outputs, and two address pins allow four devices per bus.

LP5030 has OUT0 to OUT29 (ten RGB modules, LED0 to LED9) with pins 31 to 36 unconnected; LP5036 adds OUT30 to OUT35 on those pins (LED10 and LED11). Both use the same 46-pin VQFN and the same register map.

Every output has an 8-bit colour register OUTx_COLOR, giving 256 × 256 × 256 mixes per RGB module. Every group of three consecutive outputs shares one 8-bit intensity register LEDx_BRIGHTNESS (OUT0 to OUT2 use LED0_BRIGHTNESS, and so on), so the red, green and blue of one module should go on one such triple. The intensity default is FFh, full duty, so a single-colour design can work from the colour registers alone.

The intensity register follows a logarithmic curve when Log_Scale_EN = 1 (default) and a linear one when it is 0. The curve acts on intensity only, so colour balance holds as a module dims. A custom dimming law can be made by choosing linear and correcting in software.

Each output's duty is the product of its colour and intensity values. The generator has 9 bits of true PWM plus 3 bits of dithering, in which one pulse in every eight is stretched by one LSB, for 12-bit resolution; clearing PWM_Dithering_EN (default on) leaves 9 bits. The switching frequency is 29 kHz, above the audible band.

RGB modules are spread over three phases so their pulses do not all start together, cutting peak supply current, input ripple and ceramic-capacitor singing. Phase 1 (LED0, LED3, …) holds the rising edge fixed and moves the falling edge with duty; phase 2 (LED1, LED4, …) holds the pulse centre fixed and widens both ways; phase 3 (LED2, LED5, …) holds the falling edge fixed. n = 10 modules for LP5030 and 12 for LP5036.

Setting a module's LEDx_Bank_EN bit (default 0) hands its three outputs to the bank registers: BANK_A_COLOR drives the first output of each banked module, BANK_B_COLOR the second, BANK_C_COLOR the third, and BANK_BRIGHTNESS the intensity, whatever the module's own registers hold. One write can then fade or blink many modules together while others stay independent.

RIREF sets the full-scale current of all outputs. With IREF open the outputs carry almost nothing; with IREF shorted to GND the internal limit ILIM caps each output. IMAX is 25.5 mA across the whole 2.7 V to 5.5 V supply range with Max_Current_Option = 0, and 35 mA from 3.3 V to 5.5 V with Max_Current_Option = 1.

With Power_Save_EN = 1 (default), once every LED has been off for longer than tPSM (30 ms typ) the device shuts down most analog blocks and draws 12 µA at most; registers keep their contents and stay readable. Any I2C command returns it to normal mode.
At a junction temperature of about 160 °C every output is turned off; the device returns to normal operation when the junction cools below about 145 °C.
A comparator watches VCC; below VUVF the device is held in reset and goes back to initialization.

Shutdown: entered at power-up and whenever EN is low, under 1 µA. Initialization: EN high resets every register; RESET = FFh or undervoltage also forces this state from anywhere. Standby: Chip_EN = 0, outputs off, registers kept and accessible by I2C. Normal: Chip_EN = 1. Power save: entered automatically as above. Thermal shutdown: outputs off until the junction cools.
Allow up to 500 µs after the first rising edge of EN before the first I2C access; the I2C logic is reset within 3 µs of EN falling.

Standard two-wire slave up to 400 kHz. SDA and SCL each need a pull-up. Data changes only while SCL is low; START and STOP are SDA edges with SCL high. Bytes go MSB first and each is acknowledged by the receiver on the ninth clock; a master reading the last byte answers with no acknowledge. After START the master sends the 7-bit address and a R/W bit (0 write, 1 read), then the register address, then data.

ADDR1 and ADDR0, each tied to GND or VCC, select one of four addresses 011 0000 to 011 0011. Every device also answers the broadcast address 001 1100, so one write configures all of them; a broadcast read returns valid data only if every device holds the same value in that register.

Write: START, address with R/W = 0, register address, then one or more data bytes, each acknowledged, then STOP. Read: START, address with R/W = 0, register address, repeated START, address with R/W = 1, then data bytes; the master acknowledges each byte it wants followed by another and ends with no acknowledge and STOP.

With Auto_Incr_EN = 1 (default) the register pointer steps by one after each data byte, so consecutive registers can be written or read in one transfer; the pointer runs over the whole range 00h to FFh.
LED_Global Off = 1 turns all LEDs off without changing other registers. Writing FFh to RESET (38h) restores every register to its default.

Under bank control with LED_CONFIG0 = FFh and BANK_BRIGHTNESS, BANK_A_COLOR and BANK_B_COLOR at F0h, channel 1 measures 28.68 kHz at 94.10 % duty; with those three registers at 0Fh it measures 28.66 kHz at 5.833 % duty.

VCAP needs 1 µF to GND and VCC needs 1 µF to GND, each mounted right beside the device. I2C pull-ups are usually 1.8 kΩ to 4.7 kΩ, sited at the bus master; a smaller value speeds the rising edge but slows the falling one.

VCC runs from a well-regulated 2.7 V to 5.5 V rail that can deliver the full input current. Its source resistance must be low enough that current steps at start-up or on fast intensity changes never pull VCC under 2.7 V.

Keep TJ below T(TSD); dissipation rises with the voltage left across the outputs. Place CVCAP, CVCC and RIREF next to the device with a ground plane under them. Use as much board copper as possible, since the board is the main heat path, and fill the area under the exposed pad with thermal vias. Thermal vias are filled by plating, or plugged and capped, on both sides to avoid solder voids, and solder coverage under the pad is at least 85 %. The exposed pad must be soldered for thermal and mechanical performance.
